learning: If progress rises above 0.2 with steering_oscillation near or below 0.2, the speed gain is real and the next step is the sensor lead. If oscillation rises above about 0.2, reduce kd before changing geometry.
notes: Adds wheel_radius 0.04 m, as the Builder proposed. Turn gains are scaled by 0.75 (kp 1.0, ki 0.015, kd 0.19) to match the iteration 4 yaw gain, since turn rate scales with wheel radius.
rationale: Iteration 4 (wheel_track 0.08 m, kp 1.35, kd 0.25, 7 sensors at y=0.05, 16 mm, body 0.18 x 0.12 m, mass 0.8 kg) is the best design so far at 58.5. Every run ends off_track with max_error pinned at the 0.06 m floor, and progress is 0.12 to 0.19. Line loss is now rare (oval 0, s-bend 0.95, slalom 0.85), so coverage is not the main limit. Iterations 2 and 3 show that the turn-rate levers (narrower track) helped, while a longer sensor lead and a lighter body hurt. Body width cannot widen the off-track limit. The Builder proposes wheel_radius 0.03 to 0.04 m with everything else at iteration 4 values. I accept that geometry. Turn rate is (vR - vL)/wheel_track and wheel speed scales with wheel_radius, so turn authority rises by 4/3 for the same PWM differential. To keep the yaw gain near the iteration 4 level, I scale the turn gains by 0.75: kp 1.35 x 0.75 = 1.0, kd 0.25 x 0.75 = 0.19, ki 0.02 x 0.75 = 0.015. base_speed stays at 1.5 because ground speed comes from the wheel radius, not the PWM demand. line_loss stays last_direction. Expected result: ground speed and turn rate both rise about 33 percent, so progress should move above 0.2 and completion_time should become measurable on at least one track. This is a prediction, not a measurement. The risk is higher steering_oscillation and an earlier off-track event.
